https://www.baltictimes.com/over_800_you.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Over 800 young people apply to Estonian tech school expanding to Kenya 2026-07-23 BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - The Jõhvi-founded programming school //kood is set to open its first on-site study program in Kenya this September. This week, 80 young people, selected from a pool of over 800 applicants, began an admissions program. Those who successfully complete it will secure a spot in the kood/Nairobi program, which starts in the fall. The program, supported by the Estonian Centre for International Development (ESTDEV), aims to cultivate the IT talent necessary for Kenya's rapidly developing digital economy. ESTDEV will fund 50 student placements in the kood/Nairobi program, which commences in September. "For Estonia, developing digital skills in Kenya is an opportunity to share our experience as a digital nation and in education, and to establish long-term collaborative relationships with Kenya's rapidly growing technology sector," said Katrin Winter, Head of Partnerships at ESTDEV. "Estonia's development cooperation aims not just for knowledge transfer, but for a partnership where our experience helps solve local challenges while simultaneously creating new opportunities for collaboration." According to Winter, Kenya is one of East Africa's most significant technology hubs, experiencing rapid growth in both the use of digital services and the demand for qualified specialists. "By supporting the development of local talent, Estonia is contributing to a stronger, more sustainable digital economy and laying the groundwork for new connections between Estonian and Kenyan businesses, educational institutions, and innovation communities," she added. Interest in the program surpassed all expectations, with candidates registering from across Kenya. Notably, nearly 40 percent of the applicants have no prior programming experience. The program is implemented by //kood, a technology school established in Estonia, whose graduates are employed by over 150 technology companies. The Nairobi program marks the school's first academic venture outside of Europe. ESTDEV supported the program through its Africa support fund, with a grant of 80,000 euros allocated for this new phase of the project. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gq.text: Figure caption, Plumes of smoke seen over Reno as thousands evacuate due to wildfires By Ben Hatton Â and Â Max Matza Published 24 August 2026 Updated 8 hours ago US fire crews have reported progress in their efforts to tackle a large wildfire menacing the city of Reno, Nevada - saying the blaze is about a quarter contained. The Hawk Fire, which began on Saturday, had spread over 15,000 acres by Monday, firefighters said. Evacuation orders remain in place for 23,000 people, though other residents have now been allowed to return to their homes. Tens of thousands of other residents have been told to be ready to leave at any moment. Officials are concerned that gusts of wind could drive the flames towards more homes. Unfavourable weather conditions are forecast for the next two days, meaning the fire could continue to burn during that timeframe. No deaths have been reported, though seven people have been injured. The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, spread in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains near Reno due to those same windy and unpredictable weather conditions. The immediate "go now" evacuation zone and wider "get set" area - where people are being warned to prepare to evacuate - do not extend to the centre of Reno, but they do affect large urban areas and part of a highway. Large air tankers and helicopters have been flying over the affected area dropping water and fire retardants. In their update on Monday afternoon, fire officials said the blaze had been at least 27% contained. Chief Richard Edwards, of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said those injured were four civilians and three firefighters, who suffered minor burns. Edwards added that 32 homes had been destroyed and six damaged, and that those numbers were expected to increase. Shelters have been set up in the area to take in displaced residents. While firefighters have made progress, more than two-thirds of the fire's perimeter remains uncontained. The fire is thought to have been caused by humans. Edwards added on Monday that investigators did not yet know if the blaze was set intentionally. Scientists say that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions more likely that assist the rapid spread of wildfires. Reno's average temperature has gone up by over 4C since the 1970s, faster than any other big US city, according to Climate Central. Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo earlier declared a state of emergency in surrounding Washoe County, and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said on Saturday. Firefighters from Australia and New Zealand have so far taken part in the containment effort â as well as crews from 15 US states. Image source, Getty Images Image source, Reuters/Nevada National Guard Image caption, The Nevada National Guard said 72 personnel, one Chinook and one Black Hawk helicopter had joined the response The University of Nevada in Reno - which has its main campus in the city close to the "get set" warning area - previously said regular campus operations would continue but that it was monitoring the situation. But one student, James Wolfgang Perez, said some teaching staff had independently decided to cancel their classes. The sight of the fire spreading in the direction of the campus on Saturday had been "apocalyptic", he told the BBC. Justin Davis, 29, lives on Peavine Mountain, close to Reno, and similarly watched as the fire spread towards his home on Saturday and destroyed four of his vehicles. He told the BBC he had previously bought a water truck in case a wildfire like this occurred and had used it to save his home. "We turned on the water truck and just started spraying down the things we wanted to save," he said. Image source, Justin Davis Image caption, Justin Davis, who lives close to Reno, said his neighbour's properties were "completely levelled" by the fire The blaze has been been named the Hawk Fire because it was first reported near the Hawk Meadow Trail, to the west of Reno. Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people. Wildfires are common in south-western US states, including Nevada, and are becoming more severe, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Many of these fires develop in rural and less populated areas, with only a few encroaching on population centres. Are you in the area? If it is safe to do so, share your story . https://www.dairyreporter.com/Article/20.text: ADM’s collaboration across the agrifood supply chain to incentivize farmers to shift to regenerative agriculture practices has led to over a 946,000-metric-ton reduction of CO2 emissions in 2025 ─ according to the commodity giant’s fourth annual regenerative agriculture report. In 2025, ADM supported 4.6 million acres of regenerative farmland across 11 countries, including Australia, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Germany, Hungary, India, Serbia, Poland, UK, and the US, through its Re:generations program. Additionally, the company supported a range of crops, including barley, canola, corn, cotton, edible beans, peanuts, sorghum, soybeans, sunflowers, and wheat. Nearly all (99%) of the farmers involved in the 2025 regenerative program in North America plan to re-enroll again, and 91% said the program was positive from a farm economics standpoint, per an ADM survey of 700 farmers. Additionally, 68% of farmers said that carbon intensity scores were valuable to their operations. ADM has partnered with agrifood stakeholders and consumer brands, like PepsiCo, Campbell’s, General Mills, Grupo Bimbo, The J M Smucker Co, Mars, Ooni, and Walmart. In July 2026, ADM revealed a partnership with Walmart and General Mills to help Midwest wheat farmers adopt regen ag projects, as AgNavigator reported. Additionally, ADM highlighted several other initiatives across the globe in the annual regen ag report, including: “Resilience starts on the farm. By improving and protecting soil health, farmers can be better equipped to adapt to changing conditions and maintain productive operations. That resilience can extend across the value chain, helping strengthen the food system we all depend on,” said Greg Morris, SVP and president, ag services and oilseeds at ADM, in a press release.

https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-tests-nat.text: Accessibility links Skip to main content Skip to main Navigation Skip to Search Print Options: Images Multimedia Embedded Content Comments News Analysis As Russia Tests Western Alliance, US Lawmakers Push ‘NATO Shield’ Bill By Alex Raufoglu October 03, 2026 01:13 CET As Russia Tests Western Alliance, US Lawmakers Push ‘NATO Shield’ Bill Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google WASHINGTON -- As tensions between NATO and Russia intensify amid growing fears of confrontation, US lawmakers are raising questions over the relationship between the United States and the military alliance. That is the issue at the center of a new bipartisan bill led by Democratic lawmaker Jimmy Panetta and his Republican counterpart Joe Wilson. The NATO Shield Act would require congressional approval before a president could initiate a US withdrawal from NATO. SEE ALSO: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans Panetta, in an interview with RFE/RL on October 1, argued that the measure is particularly important at a moment when Russia is testing the alliance and uncertainty surrounds Washington's future force posture in Europe. The legislation, introduced September 24, would require the president to consult Congress within 72 hours of considering a withdrawal from the military alliance and submit a report explaining the legal basis, strategic rationale, and expected consequences. Any withdrawal action would end after 30 days unless Congress approved it. Panetta said NATO is “one of the most consequential and successful security alliances in the history of the world” and argued that any fundamental change in US national security policy should not be left to the president to decide. But his argument goes beyond the possibility of a formal US withdrawal. Panetta said Russian President Vladimir Putin is already “testing” NATO through pressure, probing, and “poking” at the alliance before any potential move toward direct confrontation. He pointed to Russia's activities around the Baltic region, Poland, and other NATO border states as examples of what he described as “gray-zone” warfare. For Panetta, the danger lies partly in actions that remain below the threshold of open war. “We cannot let gray-zone warfare go unnoticed and unresponded to,” he said, warning that Russia could gradually pressure NATO members in much the same way China has applied pressure around Taiwan. “An attack on one of us will be an attack on all,” Panetta said, invoking the alliance's collective-defense principle laid out in Article 5 in NATO's founding treaty. Latvian Defense Minister: ‘Russia Will Use Any Means To Threaten Us’ by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:50 0:00 He said Putin is “not stupid,” but is “aggressive” and focused on a vision of restoring elements of the former Soviet sphere of influence. NATO, he argued, remains a major obstacle to that ambition. He pointed specifically to NATO's members in the Baltic states, saying that after visiting Estonia, he was impressed by the region's preparations for possible threats. Washington, he argued, should “turn towards the east” alongside its Baltic allies rather than allow Russia to gradually increase pressure on NATO's eastern flank. Moscow has sharply escalated its rhetoric toward NATO in recent days. Russian officials have warned that Russia could use all weapons at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, if its territory or the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad were directly threatened. SEE ALSO: Russia Launches Deadly Strikes On Ukraine As 'Hybrid Attack' Concerns Rise In The West NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has rejected the threats, saying the alliance is defensive and that nuclear threats are “not helpful.” Rutte has also said NATO sees no imminent threat to its territory while warning that Russia's activities in the region require continued vigilance. The NATO Shield Act is designed to put Congress inject into the process. The bill says withdrawal from NATO would have major implications for US exposure to hostilities, deterrence, and global military commitments. It frames withdrawal as a decision with direct war-powers implications requiring congressional participation. Wilson, Panetta's Republican co-lead, told RFE/RL on October 1 that NATO is “the backbone of the common security of Western civilization” and said the alliance must remain strengthened as it faces threats, particularly from Russia. The legislation follows Panetta's earlier efforts to establish congressional involvement in any decision to leave NATO. Its procedures would also prohibit federal funds from being used for a withdrawal that had not received congressional approval and provide expedited procedures for congressional action and judicial review. SEE ALSO: Poland Offers Financial Incentives To US As Talks On Military Base Advance, Minister Tells RFE/RL The initiative comes as the Trump administration continues to review the US military posture in Europe. Senior US administration officials told RFE/RL that Washington has “no plans” to abandon NATO allies or concentrate on leaving the alliance. But they also cited President Donald Trump and US NATO Ambassador Matthew Whitaker, who recently said Washington would “re-evaluate” relations with members that deny US forces access to bases or airspace during future operations. Broader Stakes The Trump administration is also reviewing force posture and basing across NATO territory under an “America First” approach. Reports of plans to withdraw as many as 40,000 US troops from Europe have been described by the administration as incorrect because no final plan has been made. Panetta's Republican partners have also emphasized the broader security stakes. Senator Thom Tillis, after visiting Ukraine and Poland last month, described the devastation he saw and argued that Russia remains the aggressor and Ukraine the victim. Speaking on the Senate floor on September 30, the Republican senator urged Washington to use sanctions, intelligence, and military assistance to support Kyiv. Republican Senator John Curtis said the US should help Ukraine defend itself, reinforce NATO's resolve to respond to threats against its members, impose costs on Russia's war machine, and demonstrate to China that invading neighboring countries does not succeed. Both senators argued that Ukraine has demonstrated its ability to fight and urged greater assistance with defensive munitions. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal likewise called for additional sanctions, air defense, and economic and military support after his latest visit to Ukraine. The lawmakers' concerns come as NATO allies report a broader pattern of Russian pressure, including alleged sabotage, cyber activity, drones, and other so-called hybrid operations. NATO has said such tactics are intended in part to test and divide the alliance. For Panetta, however, the immediate question is not simply whether Russia will attack NATO. It is whether the US will preserve the political and military commitment that has deterred such an attack for decades -- and whether any leader should be able to decide the future of that commitment alone. “Our diversity is our strength, but our unity is our power,” he said. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.text: Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now" By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 20 October 2026, 20:38 BST Updated 1 hour ago Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff. The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed. Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link. Russian President Vladimir Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions". Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine". Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war". Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro. Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism Published 1 hour ago Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC Published 1 day ago Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trump envoy Witkoff (L) joined Finnish President Stubb (C) and Zelensky (R) before their talks in Oslo Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now". "Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said. He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia. And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said. The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Zelensky took Ukraine's intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and influential lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia with him to Oslo. Both had earlier this month held talks in Miami with Witkoff and Kushner. Those talks were reportedly ended abruptly when the Ukrainian delegation learned that Trump had announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Zelensky had reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present" for Russian President Vladimir Putin. Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink. Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved. Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally. European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia. On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly". "It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV. Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy". "We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.
